summary: This document specifies PT-EAP, a Posture Transport protocol based on EAP, designed to be used only inside an EAP tunnel method protected by TLS. It also describes its intended applicability.

eli5.summary: Before joining a network, a device may need a health check. This is a way to carry that checkup report inside a protected tunnel.

questions: how does pt-eap prevent asokan attacks
subtitle: A tiny EAP method that carries endpoint health reports inside a protected tunnel before a device joins the network.

tldr.problem: Before an endpoint is admitted to a network, the network may want to check its posture, but there is no IP connectivity yet to carry that exchange.
tldr.mechanism: PT-EAP is an inner EAP method (type 54) that carries PB-TNC batches back and forth, and it MUST run inside a TLS-based EAP tunnel method that supplies the security.
tldr.outcome: It defines the pre-admission transport for Network Endpoint Assessment, with PT-TLS covering endpoints that already have an IP address. On its own it provides no security.

today: RFC 7171 is a Proposed Standard. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 7171 specifies PT-EAP, a Posture Transport (PT) protocol for the Network Endpoint Assessment (NEA) architecture. A PT protocol carries Posture Broker (PB-TNC) batches, often containing Posture Attributes (PA-TNC), between the NEA Client and the NEA Server.

NEA is meant for both pre-admission checks and checks of endpoints already on the network, so two PT protocols exist. PT-TLS (RFC 6876) works after the endpoint has an IP address. PT-EAP works before the endpoint gets any access to the IP network.
sections.eli5: There are two ways to deliver a health report. One is for computers already on the network. PT-EAP is for computers still waiting at the door.

sections.title: Where PT-EAP Is Used
sections.content:
PT-EAP is an inner EAP method. It is designed to run inside a protected tunnel such as TEAP (RFC 7170), EAP-FAST (RFC 4851) or EAP-TTLS (RFC 5281). The outer method is a TLS-based EAP method that first sets up the tunnel; other conversations, such as inner EAP methods, then happen inside it.

Because the tunnel gives confidentiality and message integrity, PT-EAP does not. It MUST be used inside a TLS-based EAP tunnel method that provides strong cryptographic authentication (possibly server only), integrity and confidentiality. The RFC uses the terms NEA Client and NEA Server, which correspond to the EAP peer and EAP authenticator.
sections.eli5: PT-EAP is a letter with no lock of its own. It must travel inside a locked box, which is the tunnel.

sections.title: The Two Phases
sections.content:
PT-EAP has two phases in strict sequence: negotiation and data transport. Negotiation has one message: the NEA Server sends a PT-EAP Start message, an EAP Request of type PT-EAP with the S flag set.

In the data transport phase, which is the only time PB-TNC batches may be exchanged, the NEA Client sends the first batch and the two sides then take turns. The phase ends with an EAP Response from the client, whose Data field may be empty if the server sent the last batch. Either side may abort at any time by stopping the exchange.

Success or failure of PT-EAP does not by itself decide the overall authentication. That depends on the administrator's policy.
sections.eli5: First the server says hello. Then the two sides pass notes back and forth, one at a time, until the checkup is done.

sections.title: Version Negotiation
sections.content:
The server MUST set the Version field in its Start message to the highest PT-EAP version it supports and will accept. The client picks the version and puts it in its response. It SHOULD choose the server's value if it supports it, and MAY choose a lower one. If the client supports only higher versions, it MUST abnormally terminate the EAP negotiation.

If the server finds the client's version unacceptable, it MUST end the session immediately. Otherwise the client's version is used in all later messages. This RFC defines version 1; version 0 is reserved and MUST never be sent, and values 2 to 7 may be defined by Standards Action.
sections.eli5: The server says the newest language it speaks. The client answers with a language they both know, and they use that one from then on.

sections.title: The PT-EAP Message
sections.content:
A PT-EAP message starts with the four standard EAP fields: Code (1 Request or 2 Response), Identifier, Length and Type, which is 54 for PT-EAP. PT-EAP adds Flags, Version and Data.

Only the S (Start) flag is defined; it MUST be set only on the server's first message, and that message MUST NOT contain Data. The other flag bits MUST be 0 and ignored on receipt. The Data field carries PB-TNC messages, and its length is the Length field minus the header fields.
sections.eli5: Each message has a small label on the front saying who it is from, what kind it is and what version, followed by the health report inside.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
PT-EAP relies on the outer tunnel for almost all of its protection. Its own security claims table under RFC 3748 answers No for authentication, integrity, replay protection, confidentiality and key derivation. The tunnel method must give strong authentication, integrity and confidentiality, which counters message theft, fabrication and modification.

The RFC also covers the NEA Asokan attack, a man-in-the-middle in which posture from a healthy machine is forwarded through an unhealthy one. The defense is to pass the tls-unique channel binding up to the layers above, so an External Measurement Agent can include it in its attestation. Implementers SHOULD support this, and if implemented it must be verified before other attestations are evaluated.
sections.eli5: A sneaky helper could hand in someone else's clean health report. To stop that, the report is tied to the exact locked tunnel it travels in.

sections.title: Requirements for the Tunnel
sections.content:
The tunnel method carrying PT-EAP MUST provide strong cryptographic authentication, integrity and confidentiality. The NEA requirement PT-2 asks for mutual authentication, integrity, confidentiality and replay protection of PB messages. Mutual authentication can be a server-authenticating tunnel plus a client authentication inside it.

The client always authenticates the server first, so it knows the server is not a rogue before revealing configuration details. TEAP (RFC 7170) is the mandatory-to-implement tunnel method. The tunnel method also needs to support generating the tls-unique value.
sections.eli5: The computer must check that it is talking to the real network guard before sharing its health secrets.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
IANA assigned EAP Method Type 54 to PT-EAP. The RFC also creates a top-level registry named PT-EAP Versions. With only eight values available, new entries require Standards Action.

The initial entries are 0 (Reserved) and 1 (defined by RFC 7171).
sections.eli5: A public list records that PT-EAP has its own number, 54, and which versions exist.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length in octets of the message, from the Code field.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: S (Start) flag plus four reserved bits.

messages.label: Start (S flag, Version)
messages.note: EAP Request with the highest supported version.

messages.label: Final Response
messages.note: Data may be empty if the server sent the last batch.
